sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text:
Perovskite piezoelectric material nanostructures have gained immense interest in the energy harvesting community due to their ability of converting mechanical energy into electric power in a much more efficient manner. In this paper, we first successfully synthesized $\mathrm { P b } Z \mathrm { r _ { x } T i _ { 1 - x } O } _ { 3 }$ (PZT) nanowires with unique hierarchical nanostructures o $\mathbf { f } \sim 1 0 0 \ : \mathrm { n m }$ in diameter and $6 \mu \mathrm { m }$ long, by using a facile hydrothermal process. Then a unimorph cantilever energy harvester was fabricated by bonding a mixed hierarchical PZT nanowires with polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) polymer matrix to a brass substrate. The measured open-circuit voltage from this harvester was $2 . 7 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ at its fundamental resonance $( 2 5 . 2 \ : \mathrm { H z } )$ under $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { m g } }$ root mean square (RMS) acceleration input, and the measured power density was $5 1 . 8 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ with an optimal load resistance of $2 \ \mathbf { M } \Omega$ , which is approximately 8 times larger than that of the commercial $\mathrm { B a T i O } _ { 3 }$ nanowires energy harvester on the same scale, but driven by a much higher acceleration level.

KEYWORDS: $\mathrm { P b } Z \mathrm { r _ { x } T i _ { 1 - x } O _ { 3 } }$ nanowires, hierarchical nanostructure, open-circuit voltage, power density, vibrational energy harvesting

sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Perovskite piezoelectric materials have attracted considerable attention because they can generate electrical power from ambient vibrational energy more efficiently,1, 2 such as from engine vibrations,3 direct human walking motion,4, 5 gentle air-flowing,6-9 and even tiny biomechanical movements from muscles/organs,10 which could lead to a range of important potential applications for powering sensors, actuators, implants, etc. The energy conversion efficiency of piezoelectric devices largely depends on the piezoelectric coupling coefficient of nanomaterials,11 which significantly relies on the structures formed through the synthesis processes,12 the crystalline orientation,13 and the doping elements into the host lattice.14 Therefore, the synthesis approaches should be extensive conducted for achieving high-power-density energy harvesting. These approaches can be systematically investigated by adjusting the reaction conditions for exploiting their full potential in nanotechnology applications.

Energy harvesting properties have been successfully demonstrated in the literature on many high-efficient piezoelectric materials, such as $\mathrm { Z n O } , ^ { 1 5 - 1 7 } { \mathrm { ~ M o S } } _ { 2 } .$ 1 8 NKN,19-22 lead zirconium titanate (PZT),23-29 CdTe,30 BaTiO3,31, 32 PMN-PT,33, 34 BiFeO3,35, 36 and TMCMMnCl337 . Among these piezoelectric materials, PZT ceramics is the most cost-effective candidate for its perovskite nanostructure, high electromechanical coupling coefficient, high Curie temperature, spontaneous polarization and inexpensive fabrication process.37 Thus, it has been widely used in many commercial products for powering high performance sensors and actuators.38, 39 However, it is well known that PZT ceramics has the deficiency of low flexibility, high fragility and brittleness, which makes it difficult to be applied in flexible or wearable devices.40 Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) with the virtues of elasticity, thermal stability, and biocompatibility has been widely employed as a supporting medium in various flexible devices.41, 42 Therefore, embedding the PZT nanoparticles into PDMS matrix to form a readily flexible and tailorable device, may overcome such a restriction.

For nanoscale piezoelectric materials, several typical piezoelectric nanostructures have been designed for efficiently powering small electronics. For example, vertically aligned $\mathrm { B a T i O } _ { 3 }$ nanowire array energy harvester can provide an average power density of approximately $6 . 2 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ from $1 \ g$ acceleration, which is 16 times higher than that of vertically aligned $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } } }$ nanowire arrays from the same acceleration input.17 Recently, hierarchical PMN−PT nanocomposites34 can output the maximum voltage of $7 . 8 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , which is over 2 times larger than that of the $\mathrm { B a T i O } _ { 3 }$ nanocomposite harvester 43 (3.2 V) and that of the ${ \mathrm { N a N b } } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 }$ nanoharvester44 (3.2 V). However, the novel and more sophisticated perovskite structures piezoelectric nanocomposite containing unique PZT nanostructures would have great potential for high-power nanogenerators and large-output signal with flexibility and low cost. Such as hierarchical PZT nanowires, has not been reported due to the complexity of synthesis methods. Therefore, the development of rational synthesized routes to assemble nanoscale PZT nanowires into hierarchical structures in a cost-effective manner for achieving high-efficient energy harvesting is desirable and significant, which would greatly promote their applications in nanodevices.

Herein, we reported a simple and facile synthesis approach to build PZT nanowires with unique hierarchical nanostructures under hydrothermal conditions using sodium titanate nanowires as the source. The unimorph cantilever harvesting device was fabricated by bonding mixed hierarchical PZT nanowires with PDMS matrix to a brass substrate. This piezoelectric energy harvester produced much higher output voltage and power than other reported piezoelectric nanocomposites. This is potentially a key step in developing sustainable energy technology for micro/nanodevices.

sections.heading: EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
sections.text: Reagents. All the chemicals and materials used in this work include: Titanium (IV) butioxide (TBOT, Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO), zirconium (IV) oxychloride $( Z \mathrm { r O C l } _ { 2 } { \cdot } 8 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ , Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO), ethanol (EtOH, Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO), ammonia solution $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 }$ , $2 . 0 \ \mathrm { M }$ in ethanol, Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO), potassium hydroxide (KOH, Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO), lead (Ⅱ) nitrate $( \mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 }$ , Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO), and acetic acid (Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO), were all analytical-grade purity and used as received without further purification. Distilled water was used in the preparation of all aqueous solutions.

sections.heading: Synthesis of potassium zirconium titanate nanowires as a precursor. The
sections.text:
potassium zirconium titanate nanofibers were synthesized as zirconium and titanium sources for the hydrothermal synthesis of $\mathrm { P b } Z \mathrm { r _ { x } T i _ { 1 - x } O _ { 3 } }$ . Firstly, $\mathrm { T i ( C _ { 4 } H _ { 9 } O ) _ { 4 } }$ (1.354 mL) and ${ \mathrm { Z r O C l } } _ { 2 } { \cdot } 8 { \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } }$ $\left( 2 . 0 8 \ \mathrm { \ m m o l } \right)$ ) were dissolved into $1 5 \ \mathrm { \ m L }$ ethanol under continuous magnetic stirring condition, and the ratios of Zr: Ti approximately is 3.5: 6.5, then $5 ~ \mathrm { m L }$ ammonia solution $2 . 0 ~ \mathrm { M }$ in ethanol) added into the above mixture solution under continuous magnetic stirring. Followed by the addition of KOH (28 g) pellets and $_ \mathrm { H _ { 2 } O }$ $5 0 \mathrm { - m L } ,$ ), and a white suspension was formed immediately. The white suspension was transferred into a $1 0 0 \mathrm { - m L }$ autoclave with a Teflon linear, which was heated at $2 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for $1 6 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ , and then naturally cooled to ambient temperature. The resulting white solid powders were collected by centrifugation and washed with distilled water and absolute alcohol for several times to remove residual ions. The final products were then dried at $8 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 8 h }$ for the next step using for further characterization.

Synthesis of lead zirconium titanate (PZT). In this step, potassium zirconium titanate precursor (0.2864 g) was dispersed in $1 5 ~ \mathrm { m L }$ distilled water and sonicated for $3 0 \ \mathrm { m i n }$ , followed by adding $\mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 }$ $( 4 . 0 \ \mathrm { m m o l } )$ ), then KOH pellets ( $\mathbf { \xi } _ { 1 5 } \ \mathbf { g } )$ were added directly and stirred for $1 5 \ \mathrm { m i n }$ , and finally $5 0 ~ \mathrm { m L }$ $_ \mathrm { H _ { 2 } O }$ was poured into the above mixture solution. The final mixture was transferred into a $1 0 0 \mathrm { - m L }$ Teflon lined stainless steel autoclave. The reactor was heated in an oven at $2 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for $2 4 ~ \mathrm { h }$ . After the hydrothermal reaction was completed, the reaction products were sequentially washed with a diluted acetic acid aqueous solution, water and ethanol for several times to remove residual ions and centrifugation collected. The final product was then dried at room temperature for $2 4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ .

Physicochemical characterization of the samples. The X-Ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku Ultima III) was conducted to confirm the crystallinity of hierarchical PZT nanowires. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was characterized with a Crossbeam 340 microscope (Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany). In addition, energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) was performed with an INCA Energy 350 AzTec Advanced system using a silicon drift detector (SDD) (Oxford Instruments, Abingdon, UK) for the determination of element stoichiometry.

sections.heading: Fabrication of PZT-PDMS nanocomposite unimorph. The nanocomposite was
sections.text:
made by mixing PZT nano-powder into the PDMS (SYLGARD, 184 silicone elastomer kit) matrix via sonication for $3 0 \ \mathrm { m i n }$ in order to expel the dissolved air formation bubbles. The weight percentage of PZT in PDMS was approximately $40 \%$ .45 The mixture was spin-coated on an acrylic plate and then transferred into a Cu foil substrate. The final geometry of the unimorph cantilever beam is $4 \ \mathrm { c m } \ \mathrm { ( L ) } \times 0 . 7$ cm $( \mathrm { W } ) \times 0 . 0 0 4 ~ ( $ m (H), (the photo representation of the unimorph harvester can be found in the supplementary information (SI) Figure S1). After curing in the oven at $1 2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 6 hours, silver paste was covered on the top of the nanocomposite film to function as the top electrode. Then, the resulting nanocomposite was poled at $1 \ \mathrm { k V }$ for 6 hours (TREK model 2220) at room temperature.

Electrical measurement. An electromagnetic shaker (APS-113, APS Dynamics Inc.) was used to generate mechanical vibration by accelerating the clamped end of the cantilever beam. The mechanical input energy was measured by mounting a shear accelerometer (PCB 333B32) on the root of the energy harvester. Power density measurement was performed across a series of load resistances from 0 to 10 MΩ provided by a resistance box. The electrical output signals were recorded by using an oscilloscope (RIGOL MSO1104). The photo representation of experimental setup, data acquisition, and testing processes has been provided in the SI (Figure S2).

sections.heading: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
Fabrication and characterization of the PZT nanostructures. Figure 1 shows the XRD pattern of the sample hydrothermally synthesized with the potassium zirconium titanate nanowires (see ESI Figure S3) as Zr and Ti sources. All diffraction peaks can be easily indexed to the tetragonal PZT, corresponding well with the reported data of JCPDS No. 06-0452. The strong and sharp reflection peaks indicate that the as-prepared PZT product is well crystallized.

Figure 2 shows typical SEM images of the obtained PZT sample by the hydrothermal method. Figure 2a shows that the product consisting of a large quantity of hierarchical structures. Figure 2b is a higher magnification SEM image of a randomly selected area. The sample images show a three-dimensional hierarchical structure with individual nanowires extending from cube faces directions. The length of some nanowires is up to $6 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ , and the length of each individual nanowire varies with the similar diameter of approximately $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { n m } }$ . The composition of hierarchical

PZT nanowires was determined by scanning electron microscopy-energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. As shown in Figure S4, it clearly indicates that the single hierarchical PZT nanowire is composited of $\mathrm { P b }$ , Zr and Ti elements.

sections.heading: Investigation of the influence factors for the formation of hierarchical PZT
sections.text:
nanowires. The amount of $\mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 }$ is critical to the configuration of the synthesized assembly, and thus its ratio influence on the nanostructure of the final product is investigated in detail in this experiment. Figure 3 shows the SEM images of the products synthesized with different amounts of $\mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 }$ . When 3 mmol of $\mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 }$ is added as a $\mathrm { P b } ^ { 2 + }$ source, PZT assembled with long nanorods appeared in the product, as shown in Figure 3a, b, and no particles were produced. The change of morphology is observed by further increasing the amount of $\mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 }$ in the system, and Figure 3c, d give the SEM image of the product obtained by adding 5 mmol of $\mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 }$ . The cube PZT can be obtained with the size of $2 \mu \mathrm { m }$ .

To get insight into the $Z \mathrm { r }$ and Ti ions ratio effect on the evolution of PZT nanostructures, a series of $Z \mathrm { r }$ and Ti ratios-dependent experiments were conducted. Figure 4 shows representative SEM images for the samples obtained with different Zr: Ti ratios. With no added Zr elements, the product of ${ \mathrm { P b T i O } } _ { 3 }$ consists of well-defined plate nanostructure with a rectangular outline and a side length of $5 0 0 { - } 3 0 0 0 \ \mathrm { n m }$ (Figure 4a), and the thickness of the nanoplates is approximately $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { n m } }$ (Figure 4b). When increasing the Zr: Ti ratio up to 1:9, the PZT sample shows the same nanoplate assembly but with much larger size of up to $1 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ (Figure 4c, d). It is very interesting to notice that when the Zr: Ti ratio increases up to 2:8, the obtained PZT product displays cube-like nanostructures with the size of $2 \cdot 5 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ (Figure 4e). Obviously, the surface of the cube-like structure is rugged, which is assembled by small nanoplates (Figure 4f). These results, indicate that the higher Zr concentration could be favourable for the formation of three-dimensional PZT nanocube structures. In addition, we also investigated the effect of reaction temperature on the sample morphology under the same $\mathrm { P b } ^ { 2 + }$ . As shown in Figure 5a, b, cube-like assemble with square rods of $4 0 0 \ \mathrm { n m }$ diameter and $5 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ long was obtained at $1 7 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . While increasing the reaction temperature to $1 8 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , the surface square rods grow bigger with the size of ${ \sim } 6 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ long (Figure 5c, d). Figure 5d shows the broken square rods consisting of many nanorods, and some of the rods fuse together. When the temperature increases to $2 1 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , we could find the cube-like morphology of our PZT product with many nanowires (Figure 5e, f). The results indicate that the surface of cube-like PZT nanostructure could be tuned by manipulating the synthetic reaction temperature.

sections.heading: The energy harvesting performances of the PZT-PDMS nanocomposites.
sections.text:
Figure 6 shows the schematic representation of the energy harvester device fabrication processes. First, an acrylic sheet is cleaned with deionized water and alcohol (Figure 6a). Next, the preparing the mixture solution of PZT nano-powder and the PDMS matrix with weight ratio 40: 60, then spin coat the hierarchical PZT nanowires and the PDMS mixture (Figure 6b). The detailed mixture preparation process is described in the Experimental section. Next, the composite thin film with hierarchical PZT nanowires is peeled off from the acrylic substrate (Figure 6c). It should be noted that the composite thin film can be easily detached from the acrylic substrate after curing enough time. Next, attach the composite thin film onto the brass $\mathrm { ( C u ) }$ beam with PDMS before curing (Figure 6d). The composite film can be bonded tightly by curing the PDMS. Finally, the conductive silver epoxy is covered on the top side of the PZT-PDMS film (Figure 6e).

To demonstrate sustainable power generation from synthesized hierarchical PZT nanowires, the energy harvester is subjected to a sinusoidal base acceleration generated by a permanent magnet shaker. The clamped boundary condition of the energy harvester device allows simple periodic vibration of the cantilever at its resonant frequencies. This vibration induces compressive and tensile stress on the hierarchical PZT nanowires thus generating charge by the direct piezoelectric effect, resulting in a potential difference between the two electrodes of the beam. The frequency-dependent open-circuit voltage output of the energy harvester device has been investigated, as shown in Figure 7a. Obviously, the open-circuit voltage increased with the exciting frequencies from 24.5 to $2 5 . 2 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ based on $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m } g$ root mean square (RMS) acceleration and then decreased with the continuant increasing from 25.2 to $2 6 . 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . The results indicate that sinusoidal excitation at resonant frequency of $2 5 . 2 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ yielded the highest peak to peak voltage ${ \sim } 2 . 7 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ from $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m } g$ RMS acceleration input as shown in Figure 7b, which indicates the compressive and tensile stress is maximum under its resonant frequencies $2 5 . 2 ~ \mathrm { H z } )$ when the amplitude up to maximum. The open-circuit voltage output of hierarchical PZT nanowires energy harvester at a range of RMS sinusoidal acceleration from 20 to 94 nanowires energy harvester increased with the increasing RMS acceleration. The higher voltage output is produced because the high dynamic input induces a higher alternating piezoelectric charge accumulation at the two electrodes. At this resonant frequency, the PZT-PDMS device was subjected to various accelerations thus producing the different bending strain states result in producing different output voltage. Therefore, the cantilever vibrating with maximum strain can generates maximum output voltage by increasing the amplitude of the sinusoidal acceleration at the resonant frequency. The hierarchical PZT nanowires also exhibits better performance than two-dimensional ${ \mathrm { P b T i O } } _ { 3 }$ nanoplates (Figure S5). The power output from the hierarchical PZT nanowires energy harvester is calculated by measuring the voltage, across several load resistors $\mathrm { ( R _ { L } ) }$ , ranging from 0 to $1 0 \ \mathrm { M } \Omega$ . The power output from the hierarchical PZT-PDMS nanocomposite energy harvester increased rapidly as $\mathrm { R _ { L } }$ was increased up to $2 \ \mathbf { M } \Omega$ when a peak value of $0 . 5 8 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ is reached, and then reduced as $\mathrm { R _ { L } }$ was increased up to $1 0 ~ \mathrm { M } \Omega$ . The peak power density across the optimal $\mathrm { R _ { L } }$ is calculated to be $5 1 . 8 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ from $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m } g$ RMS base acceleration (Figure 7d). This power density is 8 times higher than that recorded from the $\mathrm { B a T i O } _ { 3 }$ based energy harvester $( 6 . 2 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 } )$ ) driven by a higher base acceleration of $1 . 0 ~ g$ RMS.32 It is noticed that hierarchical PZT nanowires have a higher power density than $\mathrm { B a T i O } _ { 3 }$ , because of the following advantages. Firstly, the PZT owns higher piezoelectric constants than that of the $\mathrm { B a T i O } _ { 3 }$ and $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } } }$ , which can effectively improve the voltage output, and the special hierarchical nanostructure always makes some nanowires of the bulk parallel to the two electrodes, which makes hierarchical PZT nanowires potentially have a higher effective length strain.34 Therefore, the significant performance improvement in the energy harvester device based on hierarchical PZT nanowires are largely attributed to both the higher piezoelectric constant and the unique hierarchical structure.

sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
sections.text: In summary, we have synthesized PZT nanowires with novel hierarchical nanostructures of ${ \sim } 1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { n m }$ in diameter and ${ \sim } 6 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ long, by using a facile hydrothermal process. We have fabricated a unimorph energy harvester by bonding hierarchical PZT nanowires with PDMS polymer mixture to a brass substrate. The peak output voltage from this energy harvester was $2 . 7 \mathrm { V }$ at its fundamental resonance of $2 5 . 2 \mathrm { H z }$ , and the power density was $5 1 . 8 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 }$ with an optimal load resistance of 2 MΩ. This power density is 8 times higher than that recorded from the $\mathrm { B a T i O } _ { 3 }$ based energy harvester $( 6 . 2 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { W } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 } )$ driven by a higher base acceleration RMS. This is a key step in developing sustainable energy harvesting technical for micro/nanodevices.
